Wood cites scholars for dating the creed, but also quotes its contents and develops a chronological inference; the authorities support a premise rather than replace the argument.
Ally expressly permits postmortem assumption and offers the staged sequence as Quran-compatible rather than demonstrated; conjectural fit alone does not show selective treatment of contrary evidence.
The proposed transmission chain is speculative, but Ally frames it as a compatible possible reconstruction and does not claim it is true merely because rivals are unproved.
Wood’s exclusion of ordinary individual hallucination does not adequately establish a shared external event, but this gap is an incomplete mechanism rather than truth from non-disproof.
Wood cites a Pauline report and insufficiently establishes a shared external experience, but reliance on that contested premise does not assume the resurrection conclusion itself.
Ally notes missing independent verification but also offers source-based challenges; his speculative alternatives are not asserted as true merely because verification is absent.

The attack precedes Ally’s rejection and addresses a common Muslim account within the announced perspectives; it does not initially divert from an already stated opposing position.
Ally explicitly distinguishes two senses of crucifixion and argues which sense the denial bears; transparent semantic analysis is not a concealed shift in meaning.
Wood openly distinguishes ordinary human agency from Allah’s ultimate agency through stated parallels; questionable contextual transfer is a weak analogy, not a concealed shift in meaning.
Wood selects one disputed meaning of uppermost and retains it consistently; unsupported interpretation is not the catalog’s required mid-argument shift in meaning.
Although Ally lacks a complete method for separating revelation from additions, he offers legal context as a principled basis rather than asserting a bare favorable exception.

Comparing source-critical standards across traditions bears directly on Ally’s method and evidential consistency, even though differences in genre reduce the analogy’s force.

The Quran comparison broadens the discussion, but it directly tests whether Ally’s source-critical standards are consistent across traditions and therefore remains relevant to the methodological dispute.
Wood alleges uneven standards, while Ally identifies differences in genre and asserted purpose. The move itself does not grant Wood’s sources an unexplained exception from a shared rule.
Ally uses scholarly uptake to establish that the reconstruction is discussable, while preserving it as reconstruction rather than claiming academic prestige settles historical survival.
Ally uses scholarly lineage to show the reconstruction is a live academic proposal, not to prove it true solely because named scholars or institutions endorse it.
Wood invokes limited uptake, but also presents layered-reconstruction criticism and a conditional challenge using Ally’s own criterion; scholarly popularity is not the sole basis of rejection.

Wood mentions that Zeller’s view has not caught on, but also criticizes the layered inference from reconstructed Q and conditionally applies Ally’s own scholarly-uptake criterion; authority does not replace all reasoning.
